Terminology To be added.. Chapter 6 - Binary Trees To be added.. Terminology To be added.. Chapter 7 - Sorting and Searching Algorithms To be added.. Terminology To be added.. Chapter 8 - Hashing Terminology Indexing Perfect Hashing Minimal Perfect Hashing Hash Collision Open Addressing Closed Addressing Design of Hash function Introduction of Hashing Hashing is generally [ Indexing ] . If you have learnt what [ index ] is, you may understand it as positioning or classifying objects with duplicated meaning for a smaller size of data and better searching. Steps for Indexing Define an array with a specific purpose. Define meaning for each index in the array. Classify the input and determine the size of the array. Map the input to the array. Example of Indexing (Minimal Perfect Hashing) Given A string [foo] = "abacbdef". Precondition: there will only be alphabets inside the string. If you want to find how many 'a' occured inside the string, you may use Indexing. Define an array for storing the occurrence of letters. Each index represents an alphebet. There are a total of 26 alphabets as potential input, so the size of array will be 26. Similar to the ASCII table, we can take index [0] representing the occurrence of 'a', index [1] representing the occurrence of 'b', and so on... Loop over the string and map the character to corresponding index. However, there are still some differences between Hashing and Indexing. In Hashing, we convert ASCII char to key directly with array[i] - 'a' so that 'a' = 0, 'b' = 1, and so on... which allows us to map the data easier and faster. Hash function A function f(k) is known as defined with specific formula, it can be either One-to-one , or Many-to-one , Under this property, it can convert a large variable-sized amount of data into a small datum by transforming data into keys. A Hash table arr[ ] is an array that will be created to hold the keys after conversion. A Hash value is usually an integer that may serve as an index to an array. Example of Hash function Hashing Student ID k using Modulo, where h is the function, h(k) is the hash value of k, n is an arbitrary key. h ( k ) = k m o d n h(k) = k \bmod n h ( k ) = k mod n The size of the array will be reduced significantly due to the limited range of the modulus [0 to n-1]. Take k = 5000, n = 5, the function will be h ( k ) = k m o d 5 h(k) = k \bmod 5 h ( k ) = k mod 5 In Hash table, the value k will be updated to the index of hash value, arr[h(k)] = k h ( 5000 ) = 5000 m o d 5 = 0 h(5000) = 5000 \bmod 5 = 0 h ( 5000 ) = 5000 mod 5 = 0 arr[0] = 5000, arr[1] = 5081, arr[2] = 5072, arr[3] = 5023, arr[4] = 5014 You may now be thinking of what if the index collides, it should happen frequently as the function is many-to-one. Yes, and therefore, I am going to introduce the solution against collision. Hash Collision Collision occurs when two distinct data own the same hash value . Collisions are usually unavoidable when a large set of data is mapped into small datum. It will increase the average cost of lookup operations. Solutions to Hash Collision Open Addressing Closed Addressing Load factor represents the length of data in each index, larger load factor brings lower performance Open Addressing Place the key in other free slot when collisions occured. An index only maps to 1 key. Theoretical max load factor = 1 Advantages No size overhead apart from the hash table array Better memory locality and cache performance. Memory allocation is laid out linearly Performs better when the number of keys is known in advance and the churn is low. Example of Open Addressing: Linear Probing Quadratic Probing Double Hashing Hopscotch hashing Robin Hood hashing Cuckoo hashing 2-Choice hashing Linear Probing To be added.. Quadratic Probing To be added.. Double Hashing To be added.. Closed Addressing Place the key in the same slot even when collisions occured. An index can map to multiple keys. Theoretical max load factor = depends To achieve placing multiple keys in same slot Separate chaining using linked lists Separate chaining using dynamic arrays Using self-balancing binary search trees Advantages Easier removal Assign quicker with high load factor No issues with Clustering Example of Closed Addressing: Chaining Buckets Chaining Buckets To be added.. After dealing with collision, there will be two general types of Hashing. Minimal Perfect Hashing (Best) A hash function that maps each valid input to a different hash value. Every index is taken in the hash table. Perfect Hashing A hash funciton that maps n input keys to n consecutive hash values. But not every index is taken in the hash table. Designing Hash Functions Ideal properties Low Cost Easier and faster to compute the result Variable Range Able to transform [words], [symbols] into [numbers] Uniformity Distribute the keys evenly Minimize the chance of collisions Common types of Hash Functions Division Mid-Square Folding Radix Transformation Division hashValue = key % tableSize Try to use prime number as the hash table size to reduce collisions For non integer keys, transform them into integer with ASCII code 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 int hash ( char key[size]) { int k = 0 ; for ( int i = size; i > 0 ; i--) k += key[i]; // Sum of the ASCII // or k ^= key[i]; // XOR of ASCII return k % tablesize; } Mid-Square Transform keys into integer Sqaure the number Pick some digits from the middle to hash Take tableSize = 5 key \textnormal{key} key key 2 \textnormal{key}^2 key 2 new key \textnormal{new key} new key hashValue \textnormal{hashValue} hashValue 99 9 80 1 80 80 % 5 = 0 145 2 102 5 102 102 % 5 = 2 342 11 69 64 69 69 % 5 = 4 Folding Split key into 3 parts [ Left, Middle, Right ] as you wish, left and right should have the same size Fold keys and sum the keys Shift-folding Sum the splitted keys directly Take tableSize = 5 key \textnormal{key} key split \textnormal{split} split new key \textnormal{new key} new key hashValue \textnormal{hashValue} hashValue 5829 58-29 58 + 29 = 87 87 % 5 = 2 452642 45-26-42 45 + 26 + 42 = 113 113 % 5 = 3 1234567 123-4-567 123 + 4 + 567 = 694 694 % 5 = 4 Boundary-folding Invert the left and right part of each splitted part except middle one Then sum the keys Take tableSize = 5 key \textnormal{key} key split \textnormal{split} split new key \textnormal{new key} new key hashValue \textnormal{hashValue} hashValue 5829 58-29 85 + 92 = 177 177 % 5 = 2 452642 45-26-42 54 + 62 + 24 = 140 140 % 5 = 0 1234567 12-345-67 21 + 345 + 76 = 442 442 % 5 = 2 Radix Transformation Define same key with new radix then convert back to original radix Given $ k = 358345_{10} $ Define $ k_2 = 358345_{9} \ h(k) = k_2 \space mod \space tableSize \ k_2 = 358345_{9} = 216068_{10} \ h(k) = 216068_{10} \space mod \space tableSize $ Useful shortcut Convenient Mathematics formulas for programming Gauss Summation n ( n + 1 ) 2 \frac{n(n+1)}{2} 2 n ( n + 1 ) ​ Calculate the sum of integers from 1 to n inclusively ( a + b ) ( b − a + 1 ) 2 \frac{(a+b)(b-a+1)}{2} 2 ( a + b ) ( b − a + 1 ) ​ Calculate the sum of natural numbers from a to b inclusively To be added..
